blocks.md: **An array is a corridor of numbered lockers. Number on door = index; content inside = value. Door numbers start at 0 and never skip.**

items: Direct jump: `a[i]` opens locker i instantly — no walking needed
`vector` = same corridor that can grow a new wing at the end (`push_back`)
Insert/delete in MIDDLE? Every later locker's content must shuffle — expensive feeling to remember

blocks.label: walking the corridor
blocks.py:
a = [4, 9, 2, 7, 1]
print(a[0], a[-1])            # first & last (negative indexing!)
for x in a:                   # full walk
    print(x, end=' ')

v = [4, 9, 2]
v.append(7)                   # grow: {4,9,2,7}
print(len(v))                 # vector knows its length

items.q: Array of size n — valid indices run…
items.explain: Off-by-one guard: last legal index is n-1.

options: ALL n items shift right to open door 0

blocks.label: reverse via two hands (two-pointer)
blocks.py:
l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
while l < r:
    a[l], a[r] = a[r], a[l]   # swap ends
    l += 1; r -= 1            # walk inward

blocks.label: remove duplicates from SORTED array
blocks.py:
write = 1
for i in range(1, n):
    if a[i] != a[i-1]:        # new value discovered
        a[write] = a[i]       # compact forward
        write += 1
# write = count of unique values

blocks.md: **Write-pointer idea = keep what's good, overwrite junk in place.** Reappears everywhere: move zeros, partitioning, dedupe. Learn once, reuse forever.

items.explain: Each swap settles TWO positions; pointers meet mid.

blocks.md: Grid problems usually ask: walk row-wise (nested loops), column sums (outer=c), or diagonals (r==c / r+c==n−1). Spot which LINE the question lives on before coding.

items.q: Sum of main diagonal touches cells where…

items.title: Palindrome Array Check
items.statement: Reads same both directions? Two-pointer from ends.

solutionCode.label: two pointers walking inward
solutionCode.py:
def is_palindrome(a: list[int]) -> bool:
    l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
    while l < r:
        if a[l] != a[r]:      # one mismatch is enough
            return False
        l += 1
        r -= 1
    return True               # pointers crossed with no mismatch

items.complexity: Time O(n) — one inward sweep. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is the loop `l < r` and not `l <= r`?
followups.a: When l == r the two pointers sit on the same element, and an element always equals itself. Comparing it is harmless but pointless, so `l < r` stops one step earlier. Odd-length arrays are already handled: the middle element never needs checking.

followups.q: Could you do this by reversing the array and comparing?
followups.a: Yes, and it is still O(n) time — but it costs O(n) extra space for the reversed copy. The two-pointer version is O(1) space. Interviewers ask this to see whether you notice the hidden allocation.

items.title: Rotate Left by One, Then by K (naive)
items.statement: First k=1; then repeat rotation k times; FEEL why that becomes slow.
hints: Count shifts performed: k*n — heavy smell.

solutionCode.label: naive: rotate one step, k times

items.complexity: Time O(k·n) — the point of the exercise. Space O(1).

followups.q: You are told n = 100000 and k = 99999. How many element moves does this do?
followups.a: About k·n ≈ 10^10 — far past what runs in time. That is the smell the exercise is built to produce: the cost is driven by k, and k can be nearly as large as n.

followups.q: What is the fix?
followups.a: The reversal trick: reverse the first k, reverse the remaining n−k, then reverse the whole array. Three linear passes, O(n) total and O(1) space, independent of k. You meet it properly at L2 — the goal here is to feel why it is needed.

items.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array

solutionCode.label: read pointer scans, write pointer places

items.complexity: Time O(n) — single pass. Space O(1), compaction is in place.

followups.q: Why compare against `a[write-1]` instead of `a[read-1]`?
followups.a: `a[write-1]` is the last value actually kept. `a[read-1]` is whatever the scan just passed, which may itself be a duplicate that was skipped. On [1,1,1,2] comparing against a[read-1] still works, but the write-pointer version is the one that generalises to "keep at most k copies".

followups.q: The array must stay sorted for this to work — why?
followups.a: Sorting guarantees every duplicate is adjacent, so a single comparison against the previous kept value is enough. On unsorted input you would need a hash set and O(n) extra space.

items.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays (extra space OK)
items.statement: Third output array from two sorted inputs.
hints: i,j walkers; copy smaller each step.

solutionCode.label: two walkers, copy the smaller

items.complexity: Time O(n+m) — every element copied once. Space O(n+m) for the output.

followups.q: Why `<=` rather than `<` when comparing?
followups.a: It makes the merge stable — equal elements keep their relative order, with a’s copy landing first. That matters the moment these are records sorted by a key rather than bare integers.

followups.q: LeetCode 88 wants the merge done in place into `a`, which has trailing space. What changes?
followups.a: You walk backwards from the largest element instead of forwards. Filling from the front would overwrite entries of `a` you have not read yet; filling from the back only ever writes into slots that are already spare.

items.title: Plus One

solutionCode.label: carry propagation from the last digit

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) normally, O(n) only in the all-nines case.

followups.q: Why can you return early the moment a digit is below 9?
followups.a: Adding one can only ever produce a carry out of a digit that was 9. The first non-9 absorbs the carry, so nothing to its left can change.

followups.q: Why not convert the array to an integer, add one, and convert back?
followups.a: The digit array can be hundreds of digits long — far beyond what a 64-bit integer holds. Digit-wise carry is the only approach that does not silently overflow.

items.title: Build Array from Permutation

solutionCode.label: follow the mapping literally
solutionCode.py:
def build_array(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return [nums[nums[i]] for i in range(len(nums))]

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the output array.

followups.q: Why must this be built into a separate array rather than written back into `nums`?
followups.a: Writing out[i] into nums[i] destroys a value that a later index may still need to read. Because nums is a permutation, entry i can be referenced by any other position, so overwriting in place corrupts the source mid-loop.

followups.q: The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space. What is the trick?
followups.a: Encode both old and new values in one slot: store `nums[i] + n * (nums[nums[i]] % n)`, then divide every entry by n in a second pass. It works because every value is < n, so each slot has room for two base-n digits.

items.title: Concatenation of Array

solutionCode.label: mirror the first half into the second
solutionCode.py:
def get_concatenation(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return nums + nums          # or: nums * 2

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the doubled output.

followups.q: Is the output size O(n) or O(1) extra space?
followups.a: O(n). The result itself is 2n long. Output space is normally excluded from the "extra space" budget, but say so explicitly rather than letting the interviewer assume you missed it.

followups.q: Why write both halves inside one loop instead of two loops?
followups.a: Purely a locality choice — one pass touches `nums[i]` once while it is in cache. Both are O(n); this is the kind of detail worth mentioning but not fighting for.

items.title: Richest Customer Wealth
hints: Inner loop accumulates per row; track champion.

solutionCode.label: accumulate per row, keep the champion
solutionCode.py:
def maximum_wealth(accounts: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    return max(sum(customer) for customer in accounts)

items.complexity: Time O(rows·cols) — every cell read once. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why initialise `best` to 0 rather than to the first row sum?
followups.a: Because the constraints guarantee non-negative balances, 0 is a safe floor. If balances could be negative you would have to seed with the first row (or LLONG_MIN), otherwise an all-negative grid wrongly returns 0.

followups.q: Can this be done in less than O(rows·cols)?
followups.a: No. Any cell you skip could hold a value large enough to change the answer, so every cell must be read at least once. O(rows·cols) is the lower bound.

items.title: Largest Number At Least Twice of Others
items.statement: Does max dominate everything ×2? Find max + runnerUp in one pass.

solutionCode.label: track largest and runner-up together

items.complexity: Time O(n) — one pass tracking the top two. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why must the demotion `second = best` happen before `best = nums[i]`?
followups.a: Otherwise you overwrite the old maximum before saving it, and the runner-up is lost. Ordering the two assignments correctly is the whole trick of a top-two scan.

followups.q: Why not just sort and compare the last two elements?
followups.a: It works but costs O(n log n) for information a single O(n) pass already gives you. Sorting also loses the original index unless you sort pairs, which is more code, not less.

items.title: Diagonal Sum of Matrix
items.statement: Primary + anti-diagonal sum; avoid double-counting center on odd n.
hints: g[i][i] + g[i][n-1-i]; subtract center when n odd.

solutionCode.label: both diagonals in one loop, de-duplicate the centre

items.complexity: Time O(n) — only the two diagonals are visited, not all n² cells. Space O(1).

followups.q: When exactly do the two diagonals overlap?
followups.a: Only when i == n−1−i, i.e. i = (n−1)/2, which has an integer solution only for odd n. Even-sized matrices have disjoint diagonals and need no correction.

followups.q: This is O(n) on an n×n matrix — is that a typo?
followups.a: No, and it is worth saying out loud. There are n² cells but only 2n diagonal positions, so the scan is linear in n while the input is quadratic. You never read most of the matrix.
